get_news_article <- function(query, from_date, api_key) {
  url <- paste0("https://newsapi.org/v2/everything?q=", URLencode(query),
  "&from=", from_date,
  "&language=en&pageSize=50&apiKey=", api_key)
  
  result <- GET(url)
  
  parsed_result <- fromJSON(content(result, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8"))
  
  parsed_result$articles
}

get_news_article <- function(query, from_date, api_key) {
  url <- paste0("https://newsapi.org/v2/everything?q=", URLencode(query),
  "&from=", from_date,
  "&language=en&pageSize=50&apiKey=", api_key)
  
  result <- GET(url)
  
  parsed_result <- fromJSON(content(result, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8"))
  
  parsed_result$articles
}

text:
Task 1: Querying an API in a Tidy-Style Fashion
Connect to the news API here: newsapi.org

1.
Use GET() from the httr package to return information about a topic that you are interested in that has been in the news lately (store the result as an R object).

news_pull <- GET("https://newsapi.org/v2/everything?q=Iran&from=2026-09-18&language=en&pageSize=50&apiKey=71ce2ed6f6844a9b8c771a2b3993de20")



2.
Parse what is returned and find your way to the data frame that has the actual article information in it (check content). Note the first column should be a list column!

#Check top-level contents
str(news_pull, max.level=1)

 $ status_code: int 200
 $ headers    :List of 14
  ..- attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "insensitive" "list"

#Parse to contents

3.
Now write a quick function that allows the user to easily query this API. The inputs to the function should be the title/subject to search for (string), a time period to search from (string - you’ll search from that time until the present), and an API key.

pullFromNews <- function(subject, startdt, key) {
  
  URL <- paste0("https://newsapi.org/v2/everything?q=", as.character(subject),
                "&from=", as.character(startdt),
                "&to=", as.character(Sys.Date()),
                "&language=en&pageSize=50&apiKey=", key)
  
  pulled <- GET(URL)
  #Note: missing function inputs result in R error.
    
  if(pulled$status != 200) { return("Something broke, check requirements.") }
  else {
    parsed <- fromJSON(rawToChar(pulled$content))
    tdata  <- as_tibble(parsed$articles)
    return(tdata)
  }
}

What is meant by long format data and wide format data? Which do we generally prefer for statistical analysis?
Long data has 1 row per observation and 1 col per variable vs. wide data has multiple observations stored as different columns for a single row.
Long format data is preferred for statistical analysis.

title: ST558_HW4_Kayla
text:
17.
Return people who managed a team and were inducted into the hall of fame (regardless of their hall of fame category). Return all 9 columns used in the previous 2 questions.
Note: Summarize function drops anything not in the group_by() statement. As such, tackle the Manager data first, then join with People and Hall of Fame data. Summarize also requires collect() to be called prior to to summarizing. This means that each data element for the join must |> collect() to ensure X:Y source agreement.
Note: This code completes the full return in one big, nested join. Alternatively, each database return could be saved as its own R object (tibble), and then dplyr join could simply reference the objects.

inner_join(
  
  #Top X = Managers + names from People
  left_join(#Nested X = Managers, fully processed 
            tbl(con, "Managers") |>
              select(playerID, G, W, L) |> collect() |>
              group_by(playerID) |>
              summarize(G_managed = sum(G, na.rm = TRUE),
                        Total_W = sum(W, na.rm = TRUE),
                        Total_L = sum(L, na.rm = TRUE),
                        Career_WL_Pct = Total_W/G_managed) |>
              arrange(desc(Career_WL_Pct)),
            #Nested Y = People, just to pick up names
            tbl(con,"People") |> 
              select(playerID, nameFirst, nameLast) |> 
              collect(),
            #Nested by playerID (for left join)
            by="playerID"),
  
  #Top Y = Hall of Fame, fully processed
  tbl(con, "HallOfFame") |> 
    filter(inducted=="Y") |> 
    select(playerID, yearID, category) |>
    collect(),
  
  #Top By playerID (for inner join)
  by="playerID") |>
  #Order Variables
  select(nameFirst, nameLast, playerID, yearID, category, everything())

Task 4: Writing a function

8.
We are going to write a function to get the interquartile range of a vector, we use names = F to remove the percentages names. And add ... to allow unamed arguments for the quantile function.

getIQR <- function(v, ...){
  
  quantile(v, names = F, ...)[4] - quantile(v, names = F, ...)[2]
  
  
}



9.
Now, we are going to apply the getIQR() function to the fixed_acidity,

getIQR(wine_data$fixed_acidity)

[1] 1.3


and the citric_acid columns.

getIQR(wine_data$citric_acid)

[1] 0.14




10.
We are going to write a function to get the coefficient of variation

getCoefVar <- function(v, ...){
  
  sd(v, ...) / abs(mean(v, ...))
  
}



11.
And we apply to the fixed_acidity column,

getCoefVar(wine_data$fixed_acidity)

[1] 0.1796783


and to the citric_acid column.

getCoefVar(wine_data$citric_acid)

[1] 0.4560663




12.
We need to create a wrapper function that return the IQR and the coefficient of variation for a given vector. The output is a list with both of the values calculated.

getSummaries <- function(v, ...){
  
  list(IQR = getIQR(v, ...), Coef_Var = getCoefVar(v, ...))
  
}



13.
We apply the new function to the fixed_acidity

getSummaries(wine_data$fixed_acidity)

$IQR
[1] 1.3

$Coef_Var
[1] 0.1796783


And to the citric_acid columns.

We need to write an infix function that replace the cbind function.

`%cb%` <- function(v1, v2){

title: ST558 Homework 3
text:
If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?
We can use ../MyData.csv, typically inside a read.csv() function. The .. prefix means we go up one level from our current working directory, putting us inside myfolder
What are the major benefits of using R projects?
When an R project is created, it gets associated with a directory (folder or repo) and uses this as the projects working directory. This is very useful, because if we have this repo shared (via Github), other users can pick up the same R project and all the paths should work. This allows for organization and seamless collaboration.
What is Git and what is GitHub?
Git is the actual software that performs version contolling. whereas Github is the online hosting service for projects that utilize Git software. Version controlling allows us to save every change that occurs in our project folder, and revert back to previous saves.
What are the two main differences between a tibble and a dataframe?
Tibbles are a modern re-imagining of the data frame. When printing a tibble, we only see the first few rows/columns, whereas printing a dataframe prints everything to the console. Tibbles also force you to confront problems earlier when subsetting, as they dont do partial matching. df$colnam on a dataframe will match a column named colname, whereas with a tibble it warns you explicitly the column doesn’t exist

title: ST558 Homework 3
text:
8. IQR function
We start this task by writing a basic function to get the IQR from a vector of numbers using the quantile function

getIQR <- function(vector, ...) { # ... Allows other unnamed arguments to be passed
  
  q <- quantile(vector, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), names = F, ...) 
  # Saving this as q allows us to only have to use `quantile` once
  return(q[2] - q[1])
}

text:
If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?
You would need to specify ‘../MyData.csv’ as this is located one level up from the working directory. The ‘../’ prefix moves you up one level from current into ‘myfolder/’ where ‘MyData.csv’ lives.
What are the major benefits of using R projects?
The working directory for R projects is set to the project’s root folder. Relative file paths stay consistent no matter whose machine is being used for the project. This makes collaboration more seamless without paths breaking. Relative paths are very helpful for code sharing, and version control is also helpful for code sharing. Through an R project for version control we can clone a Git repository and manage that repository through R Studio’s terminal. Related files are self contained.
What is Git and what is GitHub?
Git is a software that tracks files, changes to those files, allows you to branch to silo work and merge code changes safely. Github is a cloud hosting platform for git repos with some additional tooling for tracking, approvals, permissions policies, etc.
What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?
Printing a tibble only prints the first several rows and size summary (#rows x #cols), whereas printing a data.frame will print all rows of that object. They differ in subsetting. Tibble does not allow for partial matching on column names with ‘$’ whereas a data.frame can partially match a column name.

text:
First we create two vectors for the values of the blood pressure pre and post-treatment measurements for 20 patients

pre <- c(130, 128, 116, 124, 133, 134, 118, 126, 114, 127, 141, 138, 128, 140, 137, 131, 120, 128, 139, 135)

post <- c(114, 98, 113, 99, 107, 116, 113, 111, 119, 117, 101, 119, 130, 122, 106, 106, 124, 102, 117, 113)




Now we assign names to the elements to easily match both subjects before and after treatment.

ns <- paste("Subject", 1:20, sep = "_") # we create the names in order for each of the subjects

#And we assign them to each of the names attributes for the two vectors

names(pre) <- ns

names(post) <- ns




Here we need to calculate the change in blood pressure for each patient.

ch <- pre - post

text:
Task 4: Control Flow Practice

1
To validate whether a blood pressure measurement is optimal (\(\leq\) 120), borderline (120 \(< bp \leq\) 130), or high (\(>\) 130). We create a new column in each data frame called status

bp_study$treatment$status <- character(20)

bp_study$placebo$status <- character(10)



2
For the treatment data frame within the list, we are going to use a loop and an if/then/else logic to assign optimal, borderline or high blood pressure classification to each subject.

for (i in 1:dim(bp_study$treatment)[1]){
  
  if (bp_study$treatment$post_bp[i] <= 120){
    
    bp_study$treatment$status[i] <- "optimal"
    
  } else if (bp_study$treatment$post_bp[i] > 130){
    
    bp_study$treatment$status[i] <- "high"
    
  } else {
    
    bp_study$treatment$status[i] <- "borderline"

}

title: Homework 2
text:
Task 4: Control Flow Practice
Working within the list, add a new field to each data frame to categorize post_bp to one of the following levels:

optimal (<= 120)
borderline (>120 but <= 130)
high (> 130)


Initialize new status column in each dataset


#update df WITHIN each list
bp_list[[1]]$status <- character(20)  #treatment dataframe, blank for 20 records
bp_list[[2]]$status <- character(10)  #placebo dataframe, blank for 10 records


Apply categories for the non-placebo group:


#For loop indexes over subject (row number)
# - bp_list[[1]] isolates the treatment df list element as a df
# - [i,3] is ith row (subject) and 3rd column (post_bp)
# - [i,6] is ith row (subject) and 6th column (status)
# - logical check on 3rd column dictates the value of the 6th column

for (i in 1:20) {
  if (bp_list[[1]][i,3] <= 120){
    bp_list[[1]][i,6] = "optimal"
  }
  else if (bp_list[[1]][i,3] <= 130) {
    #Note: >120 is implied by the if/else-if logic flow
    bp_list[[1]][i,6] = "borderline"
  }
  else if (bp_list[[1]][i,3] > 130) {
    bp_list[[1]][i,6] = "high"
  } 
  else {
    cat("Something broke at ", i)
  }
}

#review results after both loops finish executing to check for indexing


Apply categories for the placebo group:


#Same approach, except...
# - loop over 10 subjects (instead of 20)
# - bp_list[[2]] isolates the placebo df list element as a df

for (i in 1:10) {
  if (bp_list[[2]][i,3] <= 120){
    bp_list[[2]][i,6] = "optimal"
  }
  else if (bp_list[[2]][i,3] <= 130) {
    #else-if logic implies also (not <= 120)
    bp_list[[2]][i,6] = "borderline"
  }
  else if (bp_list[[2]][i,3] > 130) {
    bp_list[[2]][i,6] = "high"
  } 
  else {
    cat("Something broke at ", i)
  }
}

title: Homework 2 - ST558 Group 1
text:
First, we create two vectors corresponding to the blood pressure of 20 subjects. The first, pre_bp is pre-treatment measurements, and the second, post_bp is post-treatment measurements.

pre_bp <- c(130, 128, 116, 124, 133, 134, 118, 126, 114, 127, 141, 138, 
            128, 140, 137, 131, 120, 128, 139, 135)

post_bp <- c(114, 98, 113, 99, 107, 116, 113, 111, 119, 117, 101, 119,
             130, 122, 106, 106, 124, 102, 117, 113)




Next, we will assign names to the vector elements using this paste() function

# Initialize vector of names
patient <- paste("Subject", 1:20, sep = "_")
patient

 [6] "Subject_6"  "Subject_7"  "Subject_8"  "Subject_9"  "Subject_10"
[11] "Subject_11" "Subject_12" "Subject_13" "Subject_14" "Subject_15"
[16] "Subject_16" "Subject_17" "Subject_18" "Subject_19" "Subject_20"



# Update vector attributes
names(pre_bp) <- patient
names(post_bp) <- patient

# Confirm change
print(head(pre_bp))

Subject_1 Subject_2 Subject_3 Subject_4 Subject_5 Subject_6 
      130       128       116       124       133       134 

print(head(post_bp))

Subject_1 Subject_2 Subject_3 Subject_4 Subject_5 Subject_6 
      114        98       113        99       107       116 





We can calculate the change in blood pressure by subtracting post-treatment measurements from pre-treatment measurements.

Note: Specified as subtracting post-treatment from pre-treatment. Therefore, a positive value of diff_bp is a decrease in blood pressure post-treatment (negative = increase).


diff_bp <- pre_bp - post_bp
diff_bp

mean(diff_bp)

From this data, blood pressure decreased 17 bpm, on average, after treatment.



We can specifically determine which patients experienced a decrease in blood pressure after treatment (positive change) using the which() function

is_pos <- which(diff_bp > 0)
is_pos # values are the indeces, names are preserved

mean(positive_diff_bp)

Task 1: Basic Vector Practice
First, we create two vectors corresponding to the blood pressure of 20 subjects. The first, pre_bp is pre-treatment measurements, and the second, post_bp is post-treatment measurements.

pre_bp <- c(130, 128, 116, 124, 133, 134, 118, 126, 114, 127, 141, 138, 
            128, 140, 137, 131, 120, 128, 139, 135)

post_bp <- c(114, 98, 113, 99, 107, 116, 113, 111, 119, 117, 101, 119,
             130, 122, 106, 106, 124, 102, 117, 113)

is.vector(pre_bp)

[1] TRUE


Next, we will assign names to the vector elements using this paste() function

patient <- c(paste("Subject", 1:20, sep = "_"))
names(pre_bp) <- patient
names(post_bp) <- patient
print(head(pre_bp))

Subject_1 Subject_2 Subject_3 Subject_4 Subject_5 Subject_6 
      130       128       116       124       133       134 


We can calculate the change in blood pressure by subtracting post-treatment measurements from pre-treatment measurements.

diff_bp <- pre_bp - post_bp
names(diff_bp) <- patient

Now, we can calculate the average decrease in blood pressure across all patients

mean(diff_bp)

[1] 17


From this data, blood pressure decreased 17 bpm, on average, after treatment.
We can specifically determine which patients experienced a decrease in blood pressure after treatment (positive change) using the which() function

which((diff_bp) > 0)

 Subject_1  Subject_2  Subject_3  Subject_4  Subject_5  Subject_6  Subject_7 
         1          2          3          4          5          6          7 
 Subject_8 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_14 Subject_15 Subject_16 
         8         10         11         12         14         15         16 
Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
        18         19         20 


We can see that all patients experienced a decrease in blood pressure after treatment except for subject 9, 13, and 17. Therefore, we can make a vector that is a subset of the differences to only include subjects whose blood pressure decreased.

positive_diff_bp <- diff_bp[which((diff_bp) > 0)]
print(positive_diff_bp)

 Subject_1  Subject_2  Subject_3  Subject_4  Subject_5  Subject_6  Subject_7 
        16         30          3         25         26         18          5 
 Subject_8 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_14 Subject_15 Subject_16 
        15         10         40         19         18         31         25 
Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
        26         22         22 


Finally, we can recalculate the average decrease in blood pressure from this subset

mean(positive_diff_bp)

[1] 20.64706


From this subset of only subjects who experienced a decrease in blood pressure after treatment, the average decrease for this sample was 20.647 bpm

names(pre_treatment_vector) <- names_x names(post_treatment_vector) <- names_x


3. change in blood pressure
delta_vector <- pre_treatment_vector - post_treatment_vector


4. average decrease across group
average_decrease <- mean(delta_vector) average_decrease


5. which in group had decrease in blood pressure
which(delta_vector > 0)


6. subset the vector differences to only return those that have a positive
positive_delta <- delta_vector[delta_vector > 0] positive_delta


7. average decrease in blood pressure for those who had positive
mean(positive_delta)


Basic Data Frame Practice


——————————————–


1. create data frame object
blood_pressure_df <- data.frame( patient = 1:20, pre_bp = unname(pre_treatment_vector), post_bp = unname(post_treatment_vector), diff_bp = delta_vector )


2. return only rows where diff_bp is negative
bp_df[bp_df$diff_bp < 0, ]


3. add new column
bp_df\(under_120 <- bp_df\)post_bp < 120


4. print data frame
knitr::kable(bp_df)


List Practice


—————————————


create new data frame for placebo group
pre_placebo <- c(138, 135, 147, 117, 152, 134, 114, 121, 131, 130) post_placebo <- c(105, 136, 123, 130, 134, 143, 135, 139, 120, 124)
placebo_df <- data.frame( patient = 1:10, pre_bp = pre_placebo, post_bp = post_placebo, diff_bp = pre_placebo - post_placebo )
placebo_df\(under_120 <- placebo_df\)post_bp < 120


2. create and store list with two elements
bp_list <- list(treatment = bp_df, placebo = placebo_df)


3. access fir element using three different types of syntax
bp_list$treatment bp_list[[]] bp_list[[“treatment”]]


4. access placebo\(pre_bp
bp_list\)placebo$pre_bp


Control Flow Practice


——————————————–


1. create status column
bp_list\(treatment\)status <- character(nrow(bp_list\(treatment))
bp_list\)placebo\(status <- character(nrow(bp_list\)))


2. loop status column values
for (i in 1:nrow(bp_list\(treatment)) {
  if (bp_list\)treatment\(post_bp[i] <= 120) {
    bp_list\)treatment\(status[i] <- "optimal"
  }
  else if (bp_list\)treatment\(post_bp[i] <= 130) {
    bp_list\)treatment\(status[i] <- "borderline"
  }
  else {
    bp_list\)treatment$status[i] <- “high” } }


3. loop status column values placebo
for (i in 1:nrow(bp_list\(placebo)) {
  if (bp_list\)placebo\(post_bp[i] <= 120) {
    bp_list\)placebo\(status[i] <- "optimal"
  }
  else if (bp_list\)placebo\(post_bp[i] <= 130) {
    bp_list\)placebo\(status[i] <- "borderline"
  }
  else {
    bp_list\)placebo$status[i] <- “high” } }

text:
If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?
Since the file we want is only one folder above the current working directory, we can simply specify ../MyData.csv as the relative file path. The ../ path prefix points to one folder above the current working directory.
What are the major benefits of using R projects?
R projects support the use of working directories and version control software. Working directories establish relative paths, which eliminate the need for each user to hard-code file paths specific to their machine. Relative paths are very helpful for code sharing, and version control is also helpful for code sharing. Through an R project for version control we can clone a Git repository and manage that repository through R Studio’s terminal.
What is Git and what is GitHub?
Git a type of version control software. GitHub is an online platform for hosting and sharing Git-based projects (the actual version control actions still happen within Git).
What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?

Fancy print. A data frame prints in its entirety vs. a tibble prints the first few rows of data and a size summary (#rows x #cols).
Limited type coercion. A single column of a tibble can be accessed by [ without coercing to a vector.

title: ST558_HW3_Will
text:
If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?
You would need to specify ‘../MyData.csv’ as this is located one level up from the working directory.
What are the major benefits of using R projects?
The working directory for R projects is set to the project’s root folder. This makes it easy for when you have multiple users working on the project due to the relative file paths being consistent between machines. Pathing does not break between machines. Related files are self contained.
What is Git and what is GitHub?
Git is a software that tracks files, changes to those files, allows you to branch to silo work and merge code changes safely. Github is a cloud hosting platform for git repos with some additional tooling for tracking, approvals, permissions policies, etc.
What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?
Printing a tibble only prints the first several rows whereas printing a data.frame will print all rows of that object. They differ in subsetting. Tibble does not allow for partial matching on column names with ‘$’ whereas a data.frame can partially match a column name.

title: ST558 Homework 4 - Group 1
text:
Rewriting a nested function call using baseR chaining
Without chaining, the function looks like this (Have to read from inside out, confusing!)

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(readr)


arrange(filter(select(as_tibble(iris), starts_with("Petal"), Species), Petal.Length <
1.55), Species)

# A tibble: 37 × 3
   Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
          <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>  
 1          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 2          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 3          1.3         0.2 setosa 
 4          1.5         0.2 setosa 
 5          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 6          1.4         0.3 setosa 
 7          1.5         0.2 setosa 
 8          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 9          1.5         0.1 setosa 
10          1.5         0.2 setosa 
# ℹ 27 more rows


Using chaining, we can re-write the function like so:

iris |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(starts_with("Petal"), Species) |>
  filter(Petal.Length < 1.55) |>
  arrange(Species)

# A tibble: 37 × 3
   Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
          <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>  
 1          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 2          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 3          1.3         0.2 setosa 
 4          1.5         0.2 setosa 
 5          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 6          1.4         0.3 setosa 
 7          1.5         0.2 setosa 
 8          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 9          1.5         0.1 setosa 
10          1.5         0.2 setosa 
# ℹ 27 more rows


This gives us the same result, and is much easier to follow!



Wide format gives each variable its own column with one row per unique record. Long format gives each row a single observation so one subject spans multiple rows instead of multiple columns. Long Format is generally preferred for analysis. Modeling functions expect one row per observation so long format is more intuitive for this.

title: ST558 Homework 4
text:
Rewriting a nested function call using baseR chaining

Without chaining, the function looks like this (Have to read from inside out, confusing!)

library(tidyverse)


arrange(filter(select(as_tibble(iris), starts_with("Petal"), Species), Petal.Length <
1.55), Species)

# A tibble: 37 × 3
   Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
          <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>  
 1          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 2          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 3          1.3         0.2 setosa 
 4          1.5         0.2 setosa 
 5          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 6          1.4         0.3 setosa 
 7          1.5         0.2 setosa 
 8          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 9          1.5         0.1 setosa 
10          1.5         0.2 setosa 
# ℹ 27 more rows


Using chaining, we can re-write the function like so:

iris |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(starts_with("Petal"), Species) |>
  filter(Petal.Length < 1.55) |>
  arrange(Species)

# A tibble: 37 × 3
   Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
          <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>  
 1          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 2          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 3          1.3         0.2 setosa 
 4          1.5         0.2 setosa 
 5          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 6          1.4         0.3 setosa 
 7          1.5         0.2 setosa 
 8          1.4         0.2 setosa 
 9          1.5         0.1 setosa 
10          1.5         0.2 setosa 
# ℹ 27 more rows


This gives us the same result, and is much easier to follow!

What is meant by long format data and wide format data? Which do we generally prefer for statistical analysis?
Long format data is structured with more rows, where each row consists of one observation and each column consists of one variable. Wide format data has a single row per subject and may have more than one observation in a given row (more columns). Generally we prefer long format as most software is built to deal with data formatted this way.

section: 2. Long Format and Wide Format Data
text:
2. Long Format and Wide Format Data
Wide format gives each variable its own column with one row per unique record. Long format gives each row a single observation so one subject spans multiple rows instead of multiple columns. Long Format is generally preferred for analysis. Modeling functions expect one row per observation so long format is more intuitive for this.

For this task, we’ll need to connect to the news API here: https://newsapi.org

Use GET() from the httr package to return information about a topic that has been in the news lately

Here I chose to search for articles from last Monday regarding Panthers quarterback Bryce Young

library(httr)

my_key <- "48e8f55cb8e74372b534d5595a576d81"

  query = list(
    q = "bryce-young",
    from = "2026-09-14",
    language = "en",
    pageSize = 50,
    apiKey = my_key

)

Now write a quick function that allows the user to easily query this API. The inputs to the function should be the title/subject to search for, a time period to search from, and an API key.


query_function <- function(subject, date, api_key) {
  response <- GET(
    url = "https://newsapi.org/v2/everything",
    query = list(
      q = subject,
      from = date,
      language = "en",
      pageSize = 50,
      apiKey = api_key
    )
  )
  
  parsed <- fromJSON(rawToChar(response$content))
  as_tibble(parsed$articles)
}

Now we will create a funstion that will create the URL to get data from the News API.

get_news <- function(title, period, key){
  url <- paste(paste0("https://newsapi.org/v2/everything?q=", title),
               paste0("from=", as.character(period)),
               paste0("apiKey=", key),
               sep = "&"
               )
  
  
  info_news <- GET(url = url)
  
  parsed <- fromJSON(rawToChar(info_news$content))
  
  team_info <- as_tibble(parsed$articles)
  
  team_info
  
}

Now we will create a funstion that will create the URL to get data from the News API.

get_news <- function(title, period, key){
  url <- paste(paste0("https://newsapi.org/v2/everything?q=", title),
               paste0("from=", as.character(period)),
               paste0("apiKey=", key),
               sep = "&"
               )
  
  
  info_news <- GET(url = url)
  
  parsed <- fromJSON(rawToChar(info_news$content))
  
  team_info <- as_tibble(parsed$articles)
  
  team_info
  
}
